title: Finding a place to live
goal: Describe a home and what's in it, say which floor and which room, and build sentences that say something exists somewhere.
bekal: read rental ads and ask what matters before renting

dialogs.title: Dialog — Asuntonäyttö
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to move out of the student dorm. He views a small apartment with the owner, Mrs. Nieminen.

lines.speaker: Nieminen:
lines.id: Welcome! The apartment is on the third floor.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you. Does the building have an elevator?

lines.speaker: Nieminen:
lines.text: On. Tässä on eteinen, ja tuolla on keittiö.
lines.id: Yes. Here's the hallway, and over there is the kitchen.
lines.literal: is. here is hallway, and over-there is kitchen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Keittiössä on jääkaappi ja liesi. Onko astianpesukonetta?
lines.id: The kitchen has a fridge and a stove. Is there a dishwasher?
lines.literal: in-kitchen is fridge and stove. is-? dish-washing-machine-part?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'll take it. When can I move in?

notes: **Kolmannessa kerroksessa** — ordinal numbers take endings too, just like adjectives. *Kolmas* (third) → *kolmanne**ssa***. Notice the stem changes from *-s* to *-nne-*; this is the pattern for every ordinal from three upwards.

**Keittiössä on jääkaappi** — the "in some place there is something" structure. The place comes **first**, the thing after. It's the reverse of an ordinary sentence (*jääkaappi on keittiössä*), and the difference isn't grammar but what's being talked about: the first describes what's in the kitchen, the second says where the fridge is.
**Onko astianpesukonetta?** — questions about existence use the partial form. Just like *onko teillä teetä* in unit 6: something not yet known to exist is mentioned in the partial.

**Vuorot ovat torstaisin** — the ending **-isin** means "every": *torstaisin* (on Thursdays), *aamuisin* (in the mornings), *viikonloppuisin* (at weekends). A short, very useful ending that's rarely taught early on.

**Taloyhtiö** — the housing company of a building's owners, the body that runs almost every apartment block in Finland. It manages the shared sauna, the laundry room and their schedules. You'll see this word in every rental ad.
**Sisältyvät** — "are included". In Finland water and heating are usually included in the rent, while electricity and internet usually aren't. Ask: *Sisältyykö sähkö vuokraan?*

grammars.title: Ordinal numbers
body: Used for floors, dates, order and rankings. The first two are irregular; the rest use the ending **-s**, which becomes **-nne-** as soon as another ending is added.
after: ⚠️ *Ensimmäinen* and *toinen* have nothing to do with *yksi* and *kaksi*. Both must be learned separately — just as "first" and "second" have nothing to do with "one" and "two" in English.
Dates use an ordinal plus the month name in the partial form: *kolmastoista maaliskuuta* (March 13), *ensimmäinen tammikuuta* (January 1). You glimpsed this form in unit 5.
Floors in Finland are counted as in the US: the ground floor is *ensimmäinen kerros* (the first floor). This differs from the UK and much of Europe, where counting starts from the ground floor.

grammars.title: Existential sentences
body: The structure that says "in some place there is something". The place comes first, the verb is always *on* (singular) or *ovat* (plural), and the thing comes last.

head: Suomi
Literally
English
rows: There's a book on the table.
There's a fridge in the kitchen.
There are lots of people in the city.
There's no sauna in the basement.

after: **The verb stays *on* even with many things**, as long as they're in the partial form: *Kaupungissa on paljon ihmisiä*. *Ovat* is only used when the things are specific and countable: *Huoneessa ovat ne kirjat*.
⚠️ **In the negative, the thing must be partial**: *Kellarissa ei ole sauna**a***. An old rule from unit 7, turning up in a new place.

The difference from an ordinary sentence: *Kirja on pöydällä* answers "where's the book?", while *Pöydällä on kirja* answers "what's on the table?". What comes first is already known; what comes last is the news.

sections.title: The home and what's in it

blocks.text: *Yksiö* is a one-room apartment (studio), *kaksio* has two rooms, *kolmio* three. The number counts living rooms — the kitchen and bathroom don't count. This matters when reading ads: *kaksio* doesn't mean two bedrooms.

blocks.title: Six questions before you sign
items: *Paljonko vuokra on?* — How much is the rent?
*Sisältyykö sähkö ja nettiyhteys?* — Are electricity and internet included?
*Kuinka suuri takuuvuokra on?* — How big is the deposit?
*Onko sopimus määräaikainen vai toistaiseksi voimassa?* — Is the lease fixed-term or open-ended?
*Milloin asunto vapautuu?* — When is the apartment available?
*Saako täällä pitää lemmikkiä?* — Are pets allowed?

blocks.text: ⚠️ The rental market in Helsinki is very tight and moves fast. Good ads are often gone within hours, so a short introduction letter in Finnish — however simple — really makes a difference. One paragraph is enough: who you are, what you do, and when you can move in.

items: The apartment is on the third floor.
Does the building have an elevator?
There's no sauna in the basement.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the ordinal with the right -ssa/-ssä ending.

answers: ensimmäinen — toinen — kolmas — viides — seitsemäs — kymmenes
Pöydällä on kirja. — Keittiössä on jääkaappi. — Kellarissa on sauna. — Huoneessa on kaksi ikkunaa. — Kaupungissa on paljon ihmisiä.
Asunto on kolmannessa kerroksessa. — Onko talossa hissi? — Paljonko vuokra on? — Vesi ja lämpö sisältyvät. — Kellarissa ei ole saunaa. — Milloin voin muuttaa?
